transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-21
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Dawson (Cascade Head of Eng), Sophie Alvarez (Cascade SecOps), Liam Cho (Cascade CTO)

Summary:
Redwood AE/SE walked Cascade Financial through data handling and retention controls in Redwood: request storage toggles, logging redaction, PII scrubbing, audit logs, and KMS integrations for Private deployments. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private retention options, legal hold/export, and SOC2/ISO concerns. Agreed next steps to share security docs, demo recording, and set up a trial account with request-storage off configuration for benchmarking.

Topics Covered:
- Overview of retention & request storage toggles on Redwood API and Console
- Logging redaction and PII scrubbing features
- KMS/HSM integration and customer-managed keys in Private mode
- Audit logs, SSO/SAML and RBAC for access controls
- Differences between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private in data handling
- Demo of Console toggle and API header for request-storage=false
- Compliance and legal hold/export concerns

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: All right, thanks everyone for joining, appreciate you taking the time. I'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood side, and with me is Priya, our SE who owns privacy and infra for Private deployments.
[00:08] Priya: Hey all, hi. We'll run through the retention controls and then demo the UI and a quick API flow. There's a couple of config patterns that are important depending on whether you go hosted or private.
[00:18] Mark: Thanks, Jordan. For context, our main ask is we want to ensure customer PII doesn't persist on third-party systems. We run a mix of user support and risk/ops tools that hit LLMs for triage.
[00:28] Sophie: Also SecOps here — we need auditability and the ability to guarantee deletion for certain data classes, and we have KMS requirements.
[00:34] Liam: And cost/latency tradeoffs, if we go with request-storage off, what's the impact on debugging or caching?
[00:42] Jordan: Great, those are the right questions. Quick high-level: Redwood supports request-storage toggles at the API level — you can set request-storage=false on a request header and the platform will not persist the request body to long-term request store. For hosted we also offer a managed redaction pipeline and the Console has UI toggles. For Private we support customer-managed keys, full audit logs, and you control retention windows.
[01:05] Priya: I'll share my screen for the Console demo. (screen shares) This is the retention page — you can set global defaults, per-project overrides, and enable automatic PII redaction. The redaction uses deterministic patterns but note it's not magic — things like multi-field identifiers sometimes need custom patterns.
[01:22] Priya: Here is the 'Request storage' toggle, default on for hosted trials, but you can flip it off. When off, the request body is not written to the long-term request store. Short-term ephemeral caching still happens to support low-latency KV cache for a few seconds, but nothing is retained beyond the ephemeral window.
[01:38] Sophie: Wait, ephemeral cache — how long is that window?
[01:41] Priya: Typical is 5-15 seconds, tuned by load characteristics. It's purpose is to support immediate retries/streaming; not for analytics.
[01:48] Mark: And if request-storage is off, are logs still emitted with metadata? Like token counts, latency, but without prompt text?
[01:55] Jordan: Correct. We emit telemetry — request IDs, token counts, duration, model used, routing decisions — but we redact the prompt text. Our logs can be configured to redact PII automatically or to mask at the field level.
[02:07] Liam: How reliable is the automatic redaction? We have SSNs that sometimes get formatted weird.
[02:12] Priya: Good callout. For high-risk patterns we recommend two layers: automatic redaction plus a post-processing PII scrub pipeline you run in your VPC or sidecar. For Private customers we can hook into your KMS so sensitive tokens never leave encrypted form.
[02:27] Sophie: KMS — so you support CMEK? Customer managed encryption keys?
[02:30] Priya: Yes, for Private deployments we support CMEK with integrations to AWS KMS and external HSMs. That lets you ensure at-rest encryption keys are under your control. For hosted customers we offer envelope encryption with keys managed by Redwood, and we provide attestations and key rotation logs.
[02:45] Mark: We have regulatory requirements that require 90 days of raw request retention for some investigations, but other data classes must be deleted immediately. Can Redwood do per-route retention?
[02:54] Jordan: Yes — retention is configurable per-route and per-project. You can map routes to retention policies, e.g., route /support/chat -> 90 days, route /risk/score -> 0 days, and route /customer-ssn -> disabled/never-store. Policies can be enforced in the Console or via API.
[03:09] Priya: I'll demo the API header flow. (typing) Here's a sample cURL: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -H "X-Request-Storage: false" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat ... When we see that header we mark the request ephemeral and enforce redaction rules.
[03:26] Jordan: We also have enforcement modes — in audit mode Redwood will log the violation if a route is misconfigured; in strict mode the request is rejected if it attempts to store when policy forbids.
[03:36] Sophie: What's the default for hosted enterprise?
[03:39] Jordan: Default is audit mode with retention default to 30 days for most workloads, but enterprise can set global strict mode and per-route overrides.
[03:45] Mark: How about backups and snapshots for Dedicated? If we delete requests, do they remain in snapshots?
[03:51] Priya: For Dedicated we control backups per-customer. Deletion requests are propagated to backup lifecycle. For Private you manage backups and we provide the deletion APIs and recommended retention lifecycle so you can enforce it in your own infra.
[04:05] Sophie: Legal hold — say legal requests a hold on some user's conversation. Can we export all matching conversations even if retention is normally low?
[04:12] Jordan: Yes, we have a legal hold workflow. You can flag a subject ID and we will snapshot matching interactions to a secure export bucket for e-discovery, even if normal retention is lower. That is an account-level operation and audited.
[04:24] Liam: About audit logs — are they integrated with SIEMs?
[04:27] Priya: Yes, audit logs can stream to your SIEM via syslog or S3 forwarder, and we support structured logs with JSON events including request_id, user_id, route, action, and outcome. Sensitive fields are redacted by default.
[04:40] Mark: Can we get a copy of your SOC2 and penetration test reports?
[04:43] Jordan: Absolutely — we'll share our SOC 2 Type II and the pen test summary. I'll add that to next steps.
[04:50] Priya: Now I'll do a short live demo of a retention toggle causing immediate non-storage. (demo) I'm triggering two requests: one with storage on, one with X-Request-Storage=false.
[05:05] Priya: You can see in the Console request viewer the one with storage on shows the prompt text, and the other shows "content redacted" and the fields indicate it was marked ephemeral. There's also a note about redaction confidence.
[05:18] Sophie: That "redaction confidence" — how do we interpret it? If low, does Redwood keep the text anyway?
[05:23] Priya: No, low confidence just indicates the classifier's certainty that it found PII. In strict or compliance mode we recommend rejecting low-confidence matches or routing them to a sidecar scrubber. Redwood won't keep full text unless storage is enabled and policy allows it.
[05:36] Mark: What's the plan for retention for embeddings? We use embeddings for similarity search and those can leak content.
[05:41] Jordan: Good question. We treat embeddings as data with own retention policies — you can configure embeddings to be ephemeral, hashed, or to be stored in a dedicated vector DB under your control. For hosted customers we recommend using a customer-owned vector DB for sensitive PII use cases.
[05:57] Liam: Any performance impact when enabling strict redaction or running an external scrubber?
[06:01] Priya: There can be a small latency bump if you synchronously call an external scrubber before forwarding to the model. We recommend async post-processing for non-blocking flows, or using batch scrubbers for high throughput. For very low latency flows we do inline redaction optimized in the runtime to keep under SLO, but it depends on the model and sequence length.
[06:18] Sophie: On Private we might want all request bodies to never be stored in Redwood-managed systems — can we ensure that?
[06:24] Priya: Yes, Private gives you the option to run the request store in your VPC. In that mode Redwood's control plane still exists but request data lives in your environment encrypted with CMEK.
[06:34] Jordan: Quick competitor note — some vendors will say they "don't store prompts" but they still keep logs in plaintext for up to X days for debugging. We try to be explicit about telemetry vs request storage.
[06:44] Mark: One more question: if we turn off request storage and later need to debug a root cause in production, how do we get enough context?
[06:51] Jordan: Two approaches: 1) short-term local tracing — enable ephemeral storage for a short window or create a canary route that logs more, 2) structured telemetry — we keep trace IDs and metadata so you can link to external logs and re-run requests in a sandbox if you store sanitized prompts for debugging.
[07:05] Priya: I'll show the audit log stream config quickly. (demo) You can set up webhooks, S3 sinks, and SIEM forwarders. Each event has a schema; we don't include prompt text unless storage policy allows.
[07:17] Sophie: Can we rotate keys on demand and have logs show key rotations?
[07:21] Priya: Yes, KMS rotations are audited and we publish key rotation events in the audit logs. For Private you can rotate without Redwood involvement if keys are fully customer-managed.
[07:32] Jordan: Ok we'll open for any deeper compliance questions.
[07:35] Mark: I want to capture the exact flow to require never-store on /risk/inference. We also need a sample mapping of routes to policies for prod. Can you provide a template?
[07:44] Jordan: Yes, we have a policy-as-code starter template. I'll include that with the security docs.
[07:49] Sophie: One operational scenario — what about retained artifacts in model cache or weights that might memorize PII? Do you have mitigations?
[07:56] Priya: Models can memorize but that's model-specific. On the serving side we use KV cache isolation per request and we purge caches per SLO. We also recommend using prompt engineering to avoid providing raw sensitive PII to the model; for sensitive fields, hash or tokenize before sending. For enterprise we can offer model fine-tuning guidance or hosted private models with additional safety layers.
[08:18] Liam: Any limitations on legal export for data stored in non-US regions? We have EU data residency needs.
[08:23] Jordan: We support region-specific storage and can pin retention to region. For legal export we will follow local laws and we can work with you on export mechanics.
[08:31] Mark: Ok that's helpful. I think for next steps we'll want the security docs, the demo recording, and a trial account scoped to have request-storage default off and a few routes with 0-day retention so we can run our internal tests.
[08:43] Jordan: Sounds good. We'll do that. Any other quick questions?
[08:47] Sophie: Just minor — is there a separate cost associated with retention policies or redaction?
[08:51] Jordan: There's no charge to enable redaction toggles themselves. Storage has cost and egress policies apply; dedicated/private pricing differs — we'll include a breakdown.
[08:59] Mark: Great. Thanks everyone.

Wrap-up / Recap (last 2 minutes):
[40:00] Jordan: Recap — we'll send SOC2 and pen test summary, the policy-as-code template, a recording of the retention demo, and spin up a trial account with request-storage off for Cascade. Priya will run a sample dataset demo, Mark will confirm compliance contacts and KMS requirements.
[40:20] Priya: Action items captured in the doc; we'll follow up by end of week with access and docs.
[40:30] Mark: Thanks, looking forward to trying the trial.

End.
